newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac reassures Ukraine over NATO.
newsitem.headline: Chirac reassures Ukraine over NATO.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac assured Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Thursday that both Kiev and Moscow should have a say in the eastwards expansion of NATO to help avoid new divisions in Europe.

Chirac said after meeting Kuchma that the two had "broadly convergent views" on the idea that security in post-Cold War Europe, including NATO enlargement, should be part of a deal involving all nations affected.

"We agree on these objectives and on these procedures so that Ukraine is properly associated with implementation of the new security architecture," Chirac told reporters after lunch with Kuchma who was starting a two-day visit to Paris.

Ukraine has no plans to join NATO but wants closer ties with the alliance and creation of a nuclear weapons-free zone in eastern Europe. Unlike Moscow, which opposes NATO expansion, Kiev says no state should be able to block another's membership.

Chirac, due to meet Boris Yeltsin on Sunday in a country residence near Moscow where the Russian president is recovering from pneumonia, told Kuchma said France was concerned to avoid creating new divisions in Europe, officials said.
One aide reckoned that for Chirac, "the questions must be settled in the framework of an accord in which Russia and Ukraine take part."
The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation plans to invite one or more countries to join by 1999 at a summit in Madrid in July.
NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana will meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Brussels on February 23 for a second round of talks aimed at overcoming Russian objections.

Kuchma said that he had no doubt that France, one of the Group of Seven leading industrialised states, would back Kiev to "resolve all the problems that exist today" to ensure that the Chernobyl nuclear power plant can be closed by the year 2000.
Chirac said France would be "very active" to make sure all countries, including aid donors, keep to commitments to close the plant, site of the world's worst nuclear accident in 1986.

The Group of Seven leading industrialised states have pledged $3.1 billion in grants and credits to help Ukraine close Chernobyl. Ukraine has viewed France as a lukewarm partner, both for aid and political support.
Chirac said Ukraine was "a country with which France wants very much to reinforce its economic, political and cultural links" and praised the Kuchma's reforms.
Chirac agreed to set up a bilateral commission to increase trade between the two countries, Chirac's spokeswoman Catherine Colonna said.
